title: The hen on her eggs
hook: Ananda: keep practice warm like a hen on her eggs, and the chicks break out

segments.voice: Yesterday: eleven doors, and your line, any door, opened with clear seeing. When one way to calm didn't work, did you try another door? Day four hundred forty-five.

The Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, the Buddha's own people, have built a brand-new assembly hall. Nobody has used it yet. They ask the Buddha to be the first, to bless it with a teaching. He comes, and teaches late into the night. Then his back begins to ache. So he turns to Ananda and asks him to go on teaching, while he lies down on his right side, mindful, and rests. Ananda, with the Buddha listening, takes the floor. Today: the hen on her eggs.
screen: `A NEW HALL IN KAPILAVATTHU.` → `THE BUDDHA'S BACK ACHES.` → `ANANDA TAKES THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-third discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse on the disciple in training. Ananda speaks to Mahanama, a Sakyan noble, about someone who isn't finished yet but is on the way. They keep the precepts. They guard the senses. They eat in moderation. They stay wakeful for practice. They have faith, conscience, care, learning, energy, mindfulness and wisdom. And they can reach the four deep absorptions when they wish. Then Ananda gives a picture from any farmyard. A hen has eight or ten or twelve eggs. She sits on them properly, keeps them warm, broods them well. She doesn't have to wish: oh, may my chicks break out of their shells with their claws and beaks. If she keeps sitting, they will break out, safely, on their own. So it is, Ananda says, with someone who keeps these qualities warm. They're able to break through. The hen doesn't push the chicks. She doesn't crack the shells for them. She doesn't lie awake worrying about hatching. Her whole job is to stay on the eggs. Breaking out is the eggs' business. The same picture appears in another discourse too, where the Buddha himself uses it. And when Ananda finishes, the Buddha sits up and says: good, Ananda, good. You've taught the disciple in training well. On an ordinary Tuesday, the picture still holds. You can't force the breakthrough. You can only keep the practice warm, day after day, and trust what warmth does.
screen: `THE DISCIPLE IN TRAINING` · `PRECEPTS, SENSES, FOOD, WAKEFULNESS` · `A HEN SITS ON HER EGGS` · `THE CHICKS BREAK OUT ON THEIR OWN` · then, large: `THE HEN ON THE EGGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one practice warm. Pick something you've been doing on this path: this daily sit, a kindness, a precept, an honest word. Sit, and simply stay with the breath, the way a hen stays on her eggs. Don't check for results. Don't wish for hatching. Each time the mind wanders off to ask is this working, come back and settle down on the eggs again. The bell holds the time.
Ananda. A picture of practice: keep it warm and steady, and what's ready to break out will break out. Today's word.
Your line: the hen on the eggs. Today, do your practice even if nothing seems to happen, and leave the hatching to the eggs. Day four hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers use the hen simile to encourage steady, patient daily practice without straining for results; in MN 53 a senior disciple teaches while the Buddha rests and listens.

she doesn't need to wish; if she keeps sitting properly, the chicks break out on their own.

he lay down mindfully and listened, then praised Ananda's teaching.
the hen cracks the shells to help the chicks

fork.setup: you're a hen sitting on ten eggs. days pass and nothing happens. what do you do?
options: peck the shells open to speed things up.
give up and find better eggs.
fork.reveal: Ananda's hen keeps sitting. without wishing or forcing, the chicks break out safely when they're ready.

trapdoor: what you thought: real progress comes from pushing harder.
what it means: keep the practice warm and steady; breaking through is what warmth does, in its time.

what a scholar hears: the hen simile appears in more than one discourse, including MN 16, where the Buddha uses it of a monk who has cleared away the mind's barriers and shackles and so is able to break through.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 53, Sekha Sutta (the disciple in training)
